opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the starting observation behind Deductive Closure Training is something that I think a lot of people have noticed informally: language models are trained on enormous amounts of text, and they can often answer questions about individual facts that appear in that text, but they're surprisingly bad at keeping track of what follows from those facts. You can tell a model, or train it on, some new piece of information, and then ask it about a direct consequence of that information, and it'll give you an answer that's inconsistent with what it just learned. So the model's "beliefs," to the extent we want to use that word, aren't closed under logical implication the way we'd want them to be.

The idea of DCT is to use the model itself to fix this. Language models are actually pretty good at reasoning when you put the relevant information in context. If you give a model a statement and ask, "What else would be true if this were true?" or "What would contradict this?", it can usually generate sensible implications and contradictions. What it's bad at is doing that implicitly, in its weights, when it's just been fine-tuned on a document. So there's a gap between what the model can do in context and what it actually internalizes from training.

DCT tries to close that gap. You start with some seed statements, which might be new facts you want to teach the model, or just claims the model already makes. You prompt the model to generate a bunch of related statements: things that are implied by the seeds, things that contradict them, and so on. Then you ask the model to evaluate which subset of all those generated statements is most likely to be jointly true and logically consistent. That's a kind of global inference step, closer to finding a coherent set of beliefs than to judging each statement on its own. Finally, you fine-tune the model on the statements in that consistent set. So the model is effectively teaching itself the deductive closure of what it knows, or at least an approximation of it.

What I find appealing about this is that it doesn't require any external supervision about the implications. You're bootstrapping from the model's own in-context reasoning ability and distilling that back into the parameters. We found that it helps in a few settings: in the supervised case, where you're injecting new facts and want the model to also pick up their consequences, and in an unsupervised setting, where you're just trying to make the model more factually accurate and self-consistent by having it reconcile its own beliefs. You see improvements on fact verification and on generating text that's consistent with the facts.

More broadly, I think this fits into a bigger picture I care about: we shouldn't think of training on a document as just memorizing the strings in it. What we really want is for the model to update its whole model of the world the way a person would when they learn something. If I tell you some new fact about a person you know, you immediately update a lot of other beliefs, not just that one sentence. Current training procedures don't really do that on their own, and DCT is one attempt to get closer to that kind of coherent belief updating, using the reasoning capacity the models already have.

r001.rationale: The response describes generating implications and fine-tuning on them, but does not frame DCT as the training-time counterpart to generating related knowledge at inference time before answering a question.

r002.rationale: It says models can reason about implications when information is in context but fail to internalize those implications after fine-tuning on a document.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes using the model’s in-context reasoning and distilling the results back into its parameters.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the starting observation behind Deductive Closure Training is pretty simple. When we train a language model on a corpus, we're implicitly hoping it learns not just the sentences in that corpus but everything those sentences imply. If the training data says that some event happened in 2019, we'd like the model to also "know" that it didn't happen in 2020, that anything described as preceding it happened before 2019, and so on. And what we find empirically is that models are surprisingly bad at this. They can memorize a fact and still answer inconsistently when you ask about a logical consequence of it, or when you phrase the question differently. The knowledge they've acquired isn't closed under inference.

The other thing we noticed is that these same models are often quite good at doing the inference when you ask them to do it explicitly, at inference time. You can show the model a statement and ask what follows from it, or show it two statements and ask whether they're consistent, and it'll give you a reasonable answer. So there's a gap between what the model can derive when prompted and what it actually represents in its parameters as something it believes.

Deductive Closure Training is a way of closing that gap by having the model essentially teach itself. The procedure is roughly: you take some seed text, which could be documents from the training set, or new facts you want to inject, or even statements the model generates on its own. You then prompt the model to generate the implications of that text, the things that would have to be true if the seed were true. In some versions you also have it generate the contradictions, statements that couldn't be true. Then you ask the model to assess the consistency of this whole generated set, pick out the subset that's maximally coherent and most probable under the model's own judgments, and finally fine-tune the model on that coherent subset.

What that does is turn the model's inference-time reasoning ability into a supervision signal for its parametric knowledge. It's a form of self-supervision, but structured around logical consistency rather than just next-token prediction on more data.

There are a few things I find interesting about this. One is that it doesn't require any external ground truth. The model is using its own notion of coherence to decide what to believe. That turns out to improve factual accuracy even without labels, because inconsistency is a pretty good signal that something is wrong, and when the model resolves the inconsistency it tends to land on the correct side more often than not. The second is that it gives you a handle on knowledge editing. If you want the model to learn a new fact, you don't just fine-tune it on the sentence stating the fact. You have it generate the downstream consequences and train on those too, so the update actually propagates through the model's beliefs rather than sitting there as an isolated memorized string.

I'd also be honest about the limits. The model's inferences aren't always right, so you're to some extent amplifying whatever reasoning errors it already has. And "consistency" is a weaker notion than "truth," so a model could in principle converge to a coherent but wrong set of beliefs. In practice the gains were pretty consistent in our experiments, but I think of this less as a solved problem and more as evidence that the ability to reason about one's own knowledge is a resource we've been leaving on the table during training.

r001.rationale: It describes prompting the model to generate implications and then fine-tuning on a coherent subset, using inference-time reasoning as a training signal.

r002.rationale: It says models can derive consequences when prompted but often fail to represent or consistently apply them after training on the original facts.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says the method turns inference-time reasoning into supervision for the model’s parametric knowledge.

astra-6.text:
The basic idea is that learning a fact and learning its implications aren’t necessarily the same thing. You might train a model on the fact that every member of some organization lives in France, and separately that Alice belongs to that organization. But that doesn’t guarantee that, when you ask where Alice lives, the model will say France.

Deductive Closure Training tries to close that gap by making those implications explicit in the training process. You start with information in the training data, derive additional statements that follow from it, and then train on those statements too. In the idealized version, you’d take the deductive closure—all the consequences of what you already know. In practice, that’s far too large, so you’re working with a limited set of useful consequences.

What’s interesting is that you’re not necessarily adding new information. You’re changing how accessible the existing information is to the model. And the important question is whether that helps the model infer further consequences that you haven’t explicitly trained it on, rather than just remember the ones you supplied. Of course, you also need to check the derivations: if those additional statements don’t actually follow from the premises, you can end up reinforcing errors.

r001.rationale: The response says to derive consequences from training data and train on them, but does not characterize this as a training-time counterpart to generating related knowledge at inference time before answering.

r002.rationale: It says learning a fact does not guarantee learning its implications, but does not state that a model can derive implications from a fact supplied in context that gradient-based training on text expressing that fact fails to teach.

r003.rationale: The response discusses training on derived statements, but does not say that inference-time reasoning must be compiled into the model’s weights.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea is that there’s a difference between seeing a fact and learning all the things that follow from that fact. If you train a language model on a collection of documents, the training objective asks it to predict the text in those documents. It doesn’t explicitly ask it to work out their implications.

So deductive closure training tries to make some of those implications explicit. You take the information in your training data, derive additional statements from it, and then train on those statements as well. If one piece of text says that Alice is Bob’s mother, and another says that Bob is Carol’s father, you might generate a statement about Alice’s relationship to Carol. That gives the model a training signal for a conclusion that wasn’t written down in the original data.

Of course, computing the full deductive closure of a large collection of text isn’t practical. And with natural language, you also have to worry about whether a proposed deduction is actually valid. So this is really an approximation: generate useful consequences, check them as well as you can, and incorporate them into training.

What I find interesting about that perspective is that it treats reasoning as something that can happen during learning, too. Rather than asking the model to reconstruct every chain of inference when you pose a question, you let it do some of that work ahead of time and absorb the consequences into its parameters.

r001.rationale: It describes deriving consequences during training and absorbing them ahead of time, instead of reconstructing every inference chain when answering a question.

r002.rationale: It says training on text does not explicitly teach its implications, but does not state that models can derive those implications from a fact supplied in context.

r003.rationale: It says the model does some inference work ahead of time and absorbs the resulting consequences into its parameters.
